themes.label: Danger of liberal CV significance tests
themes.need: Someone about to run a naive cross-validated significance test needs to know why ignoring training-set-selection variability can inflate false-positive claims that a new algorithm is significantly better.

themes.label: Generalization-error and CV-estimator definitions
themes.need: Someone implementing this paper's repeated cross-validation point-estimate needs its formal definition (loss function, training/test index sets, eq. 5) and the paper's scope — uncertainty estimation rather than model selection, and the overlapping-test-set CV variant studied rather than standard disjoint-fold CV.
themes.distributed_justification: The CV-variant scope caveat (overlapping vs. disjoint test sets; future work) appears in the Section 6 conclusion but answers the same 'what does this estimator cover' question as the Section 1 scope material (relation to K-fold/LOO, not-model-selection).

themes.label: Variance structure of the CV estimator
themes.need: Someone deriving or auditing the variance of a repeated cross-validation estimator needs the covariance structure (sigma0-sigma3), the exchangeable-variable lemmas, and the proven monotonicity of Var[mu_hat_J] in J, n2, and n1.
themes.distributed_justification: Lemma 2's proof (Appendix A.1) and Proposition 2's n2-monotonicity proof (Appendix A.2) are stated in Section 2 but proved in the appendix; Note 1 justifies Conjecture 1 and Notes 16-17 clarify facts used in these same proofs — one theorem-cluster, one need.

themes.label: No unbiased variance estimator exists
themes.need: Someone hoping to plug a straightforward unbiased variance estimator into a CV-based significance test needs to know which quantities are unbiasedly estimable and why no general unbiased linear/quadratic estimator of Var[mu_hat_J] exists.

themes.label: Two practical CV-variance estimators
themes.need: Someone needing a concrete, computable variance estimate for the repeated CV point-estimate needs the two proposed estimators — the rho-approximation estimator and the conservative split-based overestimator — and guidance on when each applies.
themes.distributed_justification: Notes 2-3 (the n-odd split edge case and the independence-vs-uncorrelated sufficiency) directly qualify the conservative estimator's construction described in Section 3.2.

themes.label: Liberal/conservative framework and method overview
themes.need: Someone deciding how to interpret a CV-based confidence interval or hypothesis test needs the general liberal-vs-conservative diagnostic (the political ratio) and a comparative overview of the seven candidate inference procedures.
themes.distributed_justification: Appendix A's general liberal/conservative/political-ratio framework (defined once, referenced by every method in Section 4) and its terminology footnotes (Notes 4, 15) belong with the seven-method comparison table they ground.

themes.label: Established CV significance tests
themes.need: Someone currently using the standard t-test, resampled t-test, or Dietterich's 5x2cv procedure to compare learning algorithms needs to know how each is computed and why each tends toward liberal (over-confident) inference.
themes.distributed_justification: Notes 5-8 (McNemar link, S_L^2 bias derivation, resampled-paired-t naming, Dietterich's classification-only scope) are footnote elaborations of methods 1-3 described in the main text.

themes.label: Proposed conservative CV significance tests
themes.need: Someone looking for a less liberal alternative to standard CV significance tests needs the construction and bias direction of the paper's proposed conservative Z, pseudo-bootstrap, and corrected-resampled-t procedures.
themes.distributed_justification: Note 13 qualifies the typical training/test-size regime assumed for the corrected resampled-t and corrected pseudo-bootstrap methods described in the main text.

themes.label: Simulation study design and CI methodology
themes.need: Someone replicating this paper's simulation study needs to understand how differing n1 targets across the seven methods were reconciled and how the reported confidence intervals for reference statistics were computed.
themes.distributed_justification: The n1-reconciliation setup (Section 5 intro) is elaborated by the Table-CI estimating-function methodology (Section 5 prose pointer + Appendix A.3 derivation) and by Note 9 on parameter arbitrariness — one 'how the study was designed' need.

themes.label: Regression-problem simulation setup
themes.need: Someone wants Problem 1's regression simulation setup (sample-mean vs. linear-regression algorithms) and its resulting reference generalization-error and correlation statistics used to validate the theory.
themes.distributed_justification: The algorithm/loss definitions and the resulting Table 2 reference statistics are split by the one-sentence Problem 2 lead-in but form one simulation specification.

themes.label: Gaussian-classification simulation setup
themes.need: Someone wants the Gaussian-population classification-problem simulation setup (regression-tree vs. OLS-classifier algorithms) and its resulting reference statistics.
themes.distributed_justification: Problem 2's algorithm descriptions, its Table 3, and its Splus implementation footnotes (Notes 10-11) are separated by Table 2 (Problem 1) and by the notes-section placement, but specify one simulation.

themes.label: Letter-recognition simulation setup
themes.need: Someone wants the letter-recognition simulation setup (classification tree vs. distorted-metric nearest-neighbor) and its resulting reference statistics.
themes.distributed_justification: Problem 3's setup and Tables 4-5 are separated by the Table-CI methodology sentence (assigned elsewhere), and its Splus classification-tree footnote (Note 12) sits in the notes section — one simulation specification.

themes.label: Empirical size and power comparison
themes.need: Someone deciding which CV significance test to trust needs the empirical size and power comparison of all seven methods across the regression, classification, and letter-recognition benchmarks.
themes.distributed_justification: Note 14's explanation of the Figure 2 liberal anomaly is a footnote elaboration of the size/power findings narrated in the main text.

themes.label: Choosing the number of CV repetitions J
themes.need: Someone using the resampled t, corrected resampled t, or conservative Z procedure needs guidance on how many CV repetitions J to use, balancing power gains against test-size distortion.
themes.distributed_justification: The Section 5.2 J-study discussion is interrupted twice by embedded figure-image blocks (Pass A trash at lines 709-716 and 724-731); three spans reconstruct one continuous discussion of the J parameter.

themes.label: Choosing the number of splits M
themes.need: Someone using the conservative Z procedure needs guidance on how many data splits M to use for the conservative variance estimate.
themes.distributed_justification: The Section 5.3 M-study discussion is interrupted by an embedded figure-image block (trash, 741-746) and by the Section 6 heading/recap paragraph physically preceding Figure 13's caption; three spans reconstruct one continuous M-recommendation discussion.

Pure recap: restates t04 (no unbiased estimator exists) and t05 (two variance estimators constructed) content already covered in Section 2-3; no new information.

Pure recap end-to-end: the simulation-results sentence restates t13's findings, and the J/M/procedure-choice sentence near-verbatim restates the recommendations already given in t14 (J around 15) and t15 (M between 5-10, conservative-Z-vs-corrected-resampled-t choice); no content unique to this block.
